newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Australian shares leap to record, Tokyo ends lower.
newsitem.headline: Australian shares leap to record, Tokyo ends lower.

text.p: Australian stocks hit a record high on Thursday on positive wages figures but shares in Tokyo fell for the fourth day with the Nikkei index barely holding above the key 21,000 level, brokers said.

Elsewhere in Asia, markets completed a day of mixed fortunes. Bombay shares finished down nearly three percent, New Zealand shares gained 1.4 per cent and ailing Thai stocks lost all of Tuesday's gains.
In Hong Kong, stocks closed down 18.81 points at 12,473.56, after seesawing in a 100-point range throughout the day, chiefly due to futures-related trading, brokers said.
Dealers said most Asian markets were drifting because of a lack of news, a view echoed by brokers in Tokyo.

They said the 225-issue Nikkei average ended on a feeble tone for the fourth consecutive day on subdued market activity. Most of the fluctuations during the session came from futures-linked trade, the brokers said.
They said domestic investors were likely to stay sidelined until the new coalition government takes office and starts introducing measures to stimulate the economy.
The Nikkei closed down 78.66 points, or 0.37 percent, at 21,003.49. Its December futures finished 10 points lower at 21,090.

"Trade was thin with no firm direction, and most of the Nikkei's dips and sways were coming from arbitrage-linked activity," said Kenzo Doi, strategist at Kokusai Securities. Australian shares finished at a record high after the market opened higher in defiance of a weaker Dow and garnered strength from wages data which heightened speculation of an interest rates cut soon.
The All Ordinaries index closed up 30.9 points at 2,377.6, 11.4 points above last week's previous record close of 2,366.2.
Investors would be encouraged by the Australian market's rare show of independence from Wall Street, a dealer said.
"It indicates a belief that the Australian market is still undervalued compared to the U.S. market," he said.

New Zealand shares ended 1.4 percent higher on Thursday after getting an unexpected shot in the arm from the Reserve Bank, whose comments acted to quell the rising New Zealand dollar and curb interest rates.
The NZSE-40 Capital Index ended 32.52 points higher at 2,352.91. The New Zealand dollar ended one cent weaker at 0.7006/13.
In Bangkok, Thai stocks, which moved sluggishly throughout the session due to a lack of fresh incentives, closed 1.41 percent lower on sales by local retailers, brokers said.
The SET index lost buying sentiment seen over the past five sessions and closed 13.54 points lower at 944.51. The bourse, which was closed on Wednesday, rose one percent on Tuesday.

In Tokyo, the dollar was off its highs, capped below 113 yen as an overnight rally took a breather. Dealers said the overall feeling was that the dollar had risen too rapidly. Towards the close, it was trading at 112.82/92 yen and 1.5215/20 marks, compared with New York's previous close of 112.90/00 yen and 1.5210/20 marks. At 1100 GMT, the dollar was at 112.75/80 yen and 1.5213/18 marks.

Brent December crude futures were lower in Singapore, pushed by a sell off on NYMEX over worries about a rise in heating oil stocks in the United States. December last traded at $23.80 per barrel, down 27 cents from London on volume of 488 lots.
Bullion ended at US$383.80/384.30 an ounce in Hong Kong, against New York's previous close of US$383.60/384.10.
